caveats: `init` hỏi địa chỉ public URL; nên dùng hostname ổn định thay IP để QR trên label không hỏng khi IP đổi.
HTTPS cần thiết cho camera, offline app, push, location và các thao tác secret.
AI không tự có nếu chưa cấu hình provider; không có AI vẫn nhập dữ liệu thủ công.
Mất `KEPT_SECRET_KEY` khiến backup khôi phục được dữ liệu nhưng không khôi phục secret values.
Backup phải đặt ngoài disk chứa dữ liệu; backup password tối thiểu 12 ký tự.
MCP connector OAuth yêu cầu HTTPS public URL app bên ngoài có thể truy cập.
Các kiểm thử trực tiếp với claude.ai, ChatGPT và Claude Desktop vẫn đang pending.
Kept dùng AGPL-3.0; bản sửa đổi chạy cho người khác phải cung cấp source.

## keptinventory/kept (https://github.com/keptinventory/kept)
Description: Self-hosted, open-source inventory of everything you own and where it is. AI assistant and MCP server built in.
Homepage: https://keptinventory.info/
Language: TypeScript; license: AGPL-3.0; created 2026-09-25; last push 2026-11-08
Latest release: v1.14.6 (2026-11-07)
README (start):
A self-hosted, open-source inventory of everything you own and where it is.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  

  
    
    
  

Homes, garages and storage units; the rooms, shelves and boxes inside them; the things inside
those, with receipts, manuals, warranties and history. Self-hosted, on your own server or homelab.
Nothing leaves it unless you turn it on: no telemetry, the update check off by default, the AI
provider yours to choose.

## Try it

Nothing to install, nothing saved.

- **[Try Kept](https://keptinventory.info/try/kept/):** the whole app, with a sample household.
- **[Try the map](https://keptinventory.info/try/map/):** the 3D map, with a sample home.
- **[Host it](#quick-start-host-it):** Docker Compose or Kubernetes.

## A look around

  

- **List:** names first, each with its type; a box says how much is inside; the amber tape only
  on things with a printed label.
- **Map:** each location in 3D: floors, rooms, shelves and boxes, what's inside one tap away.
  Arranged by you, or laid out by Kept. Plan view, balconies and terraces
  ([the map](https://keptinventory.info/users/location-map/)).
- **Graph:** a location's places, boxes and things, in 2D or 3D.

### On a phone

Installs as an app. Capture, scan and search, offline too.

  
  
  
    
    
  

### Labels

A short ID and a QR code for every box. Label-printer rolls or office-printer sheets; scan one to
open the box.

  
    
    
  

## What it does

Every feature, with its page: [all features](https://keptinventory.info/users/features/).

- **Inventory.** Locations, places, boxes and things, with photos, documents, purchases, tags,
  custom fields, quantities, saved views, search, an archive for what you no longer use and a trash
  you can restore from. Furniture with compartments you can turn, merge and split. A place tree you
  can widen or collapse. Hide your Personal location if you don't use it.
- **3D map and graph.** Each location in 3D, rooms at their real size, started from a floor plan
  if you have one; its places and things as a graph
  ([the map](https://keptinventory.info/users/location-map/)).
- **Labels and scanning.** Print label sheets with a short ID and a QR code; scan one to open the
  box it is on. Scan sessions count a shelf, pack a box or move a pile in one go.
- **Lending and borrowing.** Who has what and when it's due back; borrowers need no account.
  Reminders before and after the due date, and one list of everything out
  ([lending](https://keptinventory.info/users/lending/)).
- **Kits and hand-overs.** Lend a box with everything in it; each thing comes back on its own
  record ([kits](https://keptinventory.info/users/kits/)).
- **Moving house.** Numbered boxes, a label and a contents sheet for each, tracked in the van,
  unpacked by scanning ([moving](https://keptinventory.info/users/moving/)).
- **Reminders.** Warranties, services, documents, loans and low stock: in the app, by mail, push,
  ntfy, Telegram and a calendar feed.
- **Vehicles and machines.** Readings, services, fuel and running costs.
- **The household.** Shared locations with roles and end dates, share links, stocktakes,
  condition reports, an insurance report and insights.
- **Capture.** Photograph a thing, a receipt, a label or a whole room, online or offline; your AI
  provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter, Groq, or an OpenAI-compatible server such as
  Ollama) suggests the details and you confirm them. Without one, you type them.
- **AI assistant and MCP server.** Ask in plain words; changes wait for your OK. Claude and other
  AI agents connect at `/mcp` and stay connected ([how](https://keptinventory.info/users/mcp-clients/)).
- **Home Assistant.** Install Kept as a Home Assistant app; an integration brings what's due into
  dashboards and automations ([Home Assistant](https://keptinventory.info/users/home-assistant/)).
- **Paperless-ngx.** Link documents instead of copying them; the start of a word finds one, and a
  Homebox import takes its links' titles from Paperless
  ([Paperless](https://keptinventory.info/users/paperless/)).
- **Backups you can read.** Nightly restic backups to a directory, S3 or SFTP, each with a copy
  that opens in a browser without Kept; imports from Homebox (a past import can be repaired) and
  CSV, full exports.
- **Your own network or HTTPS.** Works over plain http at home, with sign-ins as long as you set
  and more than one address; an export with secret values needs HTTPS.
- **Languages:** Arabic (right to left), English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, Ukrainian and
  Vietnamese; type to find yours, and amounts are read as your language writes them. The user,
  admin and install docs are in every language too.

  

## Quick start: host it

Docker with Compose v2. Tested on 1 GB of RAM and one CPU core, a backup during photo uploads
included; Kept and its database use about 200–400 MB
([what was tested](https://keptinventory.info/install/hardware/)).

```sh
mkdir kept && cd kept
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keptinventory/kept/v1.14.6/compose.yaml
docker compose run --rm init
docker compose up -d
```

1. **`compose.yaml`:** Kept and its database in one file; no clone, no passwords to make.
2. **`init`:** asks the address you'll open Kept at (a name such as `http://kept.home.arpa:8080`
   beats an IP address: printed labels carry it), writes `.env` and shows the setup code.
3. **Start:** the database, a one-shot bootstrap that makes the database logins and their
   passwords, the one-shot `migrate`, then Kept on port 8080 (`KEPT_HTTP_PORT` changes it).
4. **First run:** open the address, enter the setup code, create the first account. It becomes
   the instance admin. Then keep the keys off this server:
   `docker compose exec kept kept admin recovery-kit` prints them.

The camera, installing the app, push and location need HTTPS. Caddy, with a certificate for
`KEPT_DOMAIN`, and Ollama for local AI come with `compose.full.yaml`: the same file plus those
([Caddy and Ollama](https://keptinventory.info/install/compose/#caddy-and-ollama),
[HTTPS](https://keptinventory.info/install/https/)). Every step in full:
[the install guide](https://keptinventory.info/install/compose/).

- **Home Assistant:** on Home Assistant OS, Kept installs as an app with its own database, backed
  up with Home Assistant's backups ([install as a Home Assistant app](https://keptinventory.info/install/home-assistant/)):

  

  Sensors and the calendar come from the separate integration ([Works with](#works-with)).
- **Kubernetes:** the Helm chart, `oci://ghcr.io/keptinventory/charts/kept`, signed and published
  with each release ([install on Kubernetes](https://keptinventory.info/install/kubernetes/)).
- **Verify the image:** `cosign verify --key cosign.pub :`, with `cosign.pub` from
  this repository ([verifying a release](https://keptinventory.info/admin/verify-release/)).
- **Backups:** nightly, encrypted, to a directory, S3 or SFTP
  ([backups](https://keptinventory.info/admin/backups/)).

## Works with

  

- **Home Assistant:** the [kept-homeassistant](https://github.com/keptinventory/kept-homeassistant)
  integration, a HACS custom repository ([setup](https://keptinventory.info/users/home-assistant/)).
  The app runs Kept; the integration brings it into Home Assistant. App users turn on the app's
  **https on Kept's port** option first ([the app and the integration](https://keptinventory.info/users/home-assistant/#the-app-and-the-integration)).

  
    
    
  
- **Paperless-ngx:** receipts, manuals and warranty cards linked to things
  ([setup](https://keptinventory.info/users/paperless/)).
- **The rest:** [integrations](https://keptinventory.info/integrations/).

## What's next

- **Next:** [compartments on the 3D map](https://github.com/keptinventory/kept/issues/238)
- **Later:** [mobile and desktop apps](https://github.com/keptinventory/kept/issues/169) ·
  [scan a room into the 3D map](https://github.com/keptinventory/kept/issues/197) ·
  [storage furniture templates](https://github.com/keptinventory/kept/issues/238)

[Full roadmap →](https://github.com/orgs/keptinventory/projects/1) · 👍 the themes you want most.

## Licence

Kept is free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3
([`LICENSE`](LICENSE)), and every feature ships in it: nothing is held back. If you run a modified
Kept for other people, you must offer them its source. The image carries the third-party notices
of everything inside it, served at `/notices.txt`.

## Install with Docker Compose | Kept
URL: https://keptinventory.info/install/compose/#caddy-and-ollama
Description: Run Kept and its Postgres with Docker Compose on your own server or homelab, sign in for the first time, and keep the keys safe.

Skip to content
Menu
On this page
Caddy and Ollama
Install with Docker Compose

Docker Compose is the way to run Kept on one machine: Kept itself and Postgres 18 with pgvector. Caddy for HTTPS and Ollama for local AI come with a second file (Caddy and Ollama). You need Docker with the Compose plugin. Tested on a machine with 1 GB of RAM and one CPU core; Kept and its database use about 200–400 MB of it (what was tested).

Four steps, with no copy of the repository and no passwords to make:

Terminal window
mkdir kept && cd kept
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keptinventory/kept/v1.14.6/compose.yaml
docker compose run --rm init
docker compose up -d

compose.yaml works on its own, so it also pastes into Portainer, Dockge and the like (see without a terminal).

Images

Releases are published to ghcr.io/keptinventory/kept, tagged 1, 1.2 and 1.2.3, never latest; 1.0.0 is the first signed one. The same images, signed with the same key, are on Docker Hub as keptinventory/kept. compose.yaml runs the release it was published with unless KEPT_IMAGE in .env names another; init writes the version it ran as there. Verify it first if you like. To run your own build, in a checkout: docker build -t kept:local . and KEPT_IMAGE=kept:local.

What runs
Section titled “What runs”
Service	Runs
db	Postgres, and stays running
kept	Kept on port 8080, and stays running
bootstrap	once on each start, then exits: the database logins and extensions
migrate	once on each start, then exits: the database migrations
init	only when you run it (docker compose run --rm init): writes .env
Caddy and Ollama
Section titled “Caddy and Ollama”

compose.yaml runs Kept alone. compose.full.yaml is the same file plus Caddy for HTTPS (the https profile), Ollama for local AI (the ollama profile) and a split web and worker deployment, commented out. It also works on its own. To use it instead:

Terminal window
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keptinventory/kept/v1.14.6/compose.full.yaml
docker compose -f compose.full.yaml run --rm init
echo COMPOSE_FILE=compose.full.yaml >> .env
docker compose up -d

With COMPOSE_FILE in .env, plain docker compose reads compose.full.yaml, so every command in these docs works as written. Kept’s services, network and volumes are the same in both files: an install can switch at any time and keep its data.

1. Write .env
Section titled “1. Write .env”
Terminal window
docker compose run --rm init

init asks for the address you’ll open Kept at, such as http://kept.home.arpa:8080 or https://kept.example.org. Links, the QR codes on printed labels and the same-site check are built from it, so it must be exactly what the browser shows, and it should not change: use a name rather than an IP address. A home router can give this machine a new address one day, and the labels you printed would then point nowhere. Set the name in your router’s DNS, or in the hosts file of each device. An IP address still works if you confirm it.

It then writes .env next to compose.yaml with that address (KEPT_PUBLIC_URL), the port (KEPT_HTTP_PORT, from an http:// address), the image and a setup code (KEPT_SETUP_CODE), and shows the code. .env holds no password and is readable by you only. Run init again to change the address: it updates those lines and keeps everything else you added. Without a terminal, give the address on the command line: docker compose run --rm init --url http://kept.home.arpa:8080.

Everything else is optional; compose.env.example and the configuration reference say what each variable does.

2. Start it
Section titled “2. Start it”
Terminal window
docker compose up -d

Compose starts the database and waits for it to be healthy. Then:

bootstrap (one-shot, kept bootstrap) makes Kept’s four database logins and the pg_trgm, unaccent and vector extensions. On the first start it generates each login’s password into a volume; on every start it sets each login’s password to that value, so Postgres and Kept always agree.
migrate (one-shot, kept migrate) applies the database migrations once, under a lock.
Kept starts on port 8080 (KEPT_HTTP_PORT changes the host port).
3. Finish setup
Section titled “3. Finish setup”

Open the address, enter the setup code init showed, and create the first account: it becomes the instance admin. Kept also prints the code in its log on its first start:

Terminal window
docker compose logs kept | grep "KEPT SETUP CODE"

A lost code is issued again with:

Terminal window
docker compose run --rm migrate admin setup-code

Wrong codes lock out for a while, per address and for the whole instance. If Kept sits behind a proxy it doesn’t trust, everyone shares the proxy’s address; see reverse proxies.

4. Keep the keys
Section titled “4. Keep the keys”

On first start, with KEPT_SECRET_KEY and KEPT_AUTH_SECRET unset, Kept generates both into the kept-config volume and logs one line saying where. The secret key seals every secret value (AI keys, the passwords you store in Kept): a backup restores everything except those values unless you also have the key.

Print the keys and keep them somewhere other than this server, such as a password manager:

Terminal window
docker compose exec kept kept admin recovery-kit

Admin → Status asks you to acknowledge the recovery kit, and Kept requires it before the first secret value, AI key or backup setting. See the recovery kit.

5. Next
Section titled “5. Next”
Put Kept on HTTPS: the camera, installing the app, push notifications and location only work over HTTPS.
Set up backups.
Mail: set KEPT_SMTP_URL (smtp:// or smtps://, with credentials) and KEPT_SMTP_FROM for password resets, invitations and reminders by email. Without them, reminders reach people in the app only, and Admin → Status says mail isn’t configured.
What Compose creates
Section titled “What Compose creates”
Volume	Holds	Back it up?
kept-db	the Postgres database	through Kept’s backup, never by copying the volume while it runs
kept-data	uploaded files (with KEPT_STORAGE=local, the default)	through Kept’s backup
kept-config	the generated KEPT_SECRET_KEY and KEPT_AUTH_SECRET, and the passwords of the kept_app, kept_auth and kept_system logins	keep the recovery kit; the passwords are made again if lost
kept-owner	the password of the kept_owner login	no; it is made again if lost
caddy-data, caddy-config	Caddy’s certificates (compose.full.yaml’s https profile)	no; Caddy gets new ones

The database’s superuser has no password anyone needs: it is reached only from inside the database container, as docker compose exec db psql -U postgres, and by the bootstrap, which shares that container’s network. Over the network every login needs its password. Never publish the db service’s port (no ports: on it): Kept reaches it over the compose network.

Kept’s containers run as a non-root user (uid 10001) with a read-only root filesystem, every Linux capability dropped and no-new-privileges. The migrate service holds the database owner’s login; the serving container never sees it (the kept-owner volume isn’t mounted there) until you give it one for the nightly backup (backups). init is the one exception to the non-root rule: it runs as root, with no network and only the capabilities that create .env in your folder and give it to you, and exits.

Without a terminal
Section titled “Without a terminal”

Portainer, Dockge and similar tools take compose.yaml (or compose.full.yaml) as it is. They don’t run init, so set two variables in their environment editor instead: KEPT_PUBLIC_URL (the address, as above) and KEPT_SETUP_CODE (six characters of 0–9 and A–Z without I, L, O and U, such as KPT-2X9; or leave it empty and read the code from Kept’s log). Pin KEPT_IMAGE to a release if the tool doesn’t.

An install from before 1.13.0
Section titled “An install from before 1.13.0”

An install made with a copy of the repository has the five KEPT_DB_*_PASSWORD lines in .env. With this compose.yaml they are used exactly as given, and nothing is generated: update the checkout (or download the new compose.yaml next to the old .env) and run docker compose up -d. Removing those lines later, or writing .env again with init, is safe too: the next start generates new passwords and sets them in Postgres. An empty KEPT_IMAGE used to build the checkout; it now runs the release compose.yaml names, so set KEPT_IMAGE=kept:local if you build your own.

Web and worker on their own
Section titled “Web and worker on their own”

One container serves the web app and runs the background jobs (KEPT_ROLE=all, the default). To split them, run a second Kept service with KEPT_ROLE=worker beside one with KEPT_ROLE=web. A worker serves no HTTP; the image’s healthcheck follows KEPT_ROLE and checks the worker’s job loop instead, so neither needs an override (compose.full.yaml has the two services commented out). The worker runs the nightly backup, so it is the one that needs the owner login and a directory target’s mount.

## Put Kept on HTTPS | Kept
URL: https://keptinventory.info/install/https/
Description: Why Kept wants HTTPS, and how to get it - Caddy from compose.full.yaml, Tailscale, NetBird, Twingate, Cloudflare Tunnel or your own proxy.

Skip to content
Menu
On this page
Overview
Put Kept on HTTPS

Kept works over plain HTTP, but a phone treats a plain-HTTP address as unsafe, and several things stop working:

the camera (Kept falls back to a file picker),
installing Kept to the home screen, and working offline from it,
push notifications,
location.

localhost counts as safe; a LAN address over HTTP does not. With an https: KEPT_PUBLIC_URL, Kept also marks its cookies Secure and sends HSTS; KEPT_HSTS=off clears it when plain-http services share the hostname (HSTS).

Some things Kept refuses outright while KEPT_PUBLIC_URL is http:, even on localhost, because they hand out or change a secret: showing a secret value, an export with secret values, opening an export’s secrets when importing it, making an access token in the browser, connecting an app with OAuth, downloading the recovery kit, and changing or testing the backup settings. An export without secret values works, and so does an import without them. Sessions are also shorter over HTTP. While Kept is served over HTTP, the Get started checklist on Home puts “Put Kept on HTTPS” first, until an admin chooses “Staying on my home network”. Everything that works over plain HTTP, in one table: Kept on a home network.

Whichever way you choose, set KEPT_PUBLIC_URL to the https:// address people will open, and restart Kept.

Compose’s Caddy profile
Section titled “Compose’s Caddy profile”

For a domain name that points at this machine, with ports 80 and 443 reachable from the internet (Caddy proves the domain to Let’s Encrypt or ZeroSSL over them). Caddy comes with compose.full.yaml, not compose.yaml (Caddy and Ollama):

Terminal window
# in .env
COMPOSE_FILE=compose.full.yaml
KEPT_DOMAIN=kept.example.org
KEPT_PUBLIC_URL=https://kept.example.org

Caddy reads docker/caddy/Caddyfile next to the Compose file. A checkout of the repository has both files; an install without one downloads them once:

Terminal window
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keptinventory/kept/v1.14.6/compose.full.yaml
mkdir -p docker/caddy
curl -fsSLo docker/caddy/Caddyfile https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keptinventory/kept/v1.14.6/docker/caddy/Caddyfile
docker compose --profile https up -d

Without the file, docker compose --profile https up -d stops with “bind source path does not exist”. Any other proxy works instead; it forwards to Kept’s port, as in the sections below.

Caddy gets and renews the certificate and forwards everything to Kept. Compose gives Caddy a fixed address on its own network and passes that address to Kept as KEPT_TRUSTED_PROXIES, so Kept believes Caddy’s X-Forwarded-For and nothing else’s. You can then bind plain HTTP to loopback only, with KEPT_HTTP_PORT=127.0.0.1:8080.

If 172.29.72.0/24 clashes with your LAN, change the network’s subnet, its ip_range, Caddy’s ipv4_address and KEPT_TRUSTED_PROXIES together in compose.full.yaml.

Tailscale
Section titled “Tailscale”

For a Kept that only your own devices reach, with no port open to the internet: on the machine running Kept, with HTTPS certificates enabled for your tailnet,

Terminal window
tailscale serve --bg 8080

serves Kept at https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net with a real certificate, to any device on the tailnet. Set KEPT_PUBLIC_URL to that address.

Tailscale’s proxy runs on the same machine and connects to Kept from 127.0.0.1; Kept sees every request as coming from there unless you trust it. On a single-household instance that only matters for the setup lockout.

NetBird
Section titled “NetBird”

NetBird’s reverse proxy gives a peer’s port a public https:// address with a certificate:

Terminal window
netbird expose 8080

It prints the address. Set KEPT_PUBLIC_URL to it (or to your own domain, with --with-custom-domain kept.example.org, set up in NetBird first). The address is public unless you choose NetBird-Only Access for the service in the dashboard, which limits it to your peers. An account admin turns on Peer Expose under Settings → Clients first.

Twingate
Section titled “Twingate”

Twingate makes Kept reachable to your devices without opening a port, but the certificate is yours: give Kept a hostname on a domain you own (kept.example.org), get a certificate for it with a DNS challenge (Caddy, Traefik or cert-manager can), and add that hostname as a Twingate resource. Set KEPT_PUBLIC_URL to https://kept.example.org.

Cloudflare Tunnel
Section titled “Cloudflare Tunnel”

For a public address with no open port. Cloudflare serves the hostname over HTTPS and forwards to Kept through cloudflared:

Terminal window
cloudflared tunnel login
cloudflared tunnel create kept
cloudflared tunnel route dns kept kept.example.org
cloudflared tunnel run kept

with ~/.cloudflared/config.yml:

tunnel: kept
credentials-file: <home>/.cloudflared/<tunnel id>.json
ingress:
  - hostname: kept.example.org
    service: http://localhost:8080
  - service: http_status:404

Set KEPT_PUBLIC_URL to https://kept.example.org. Cloudflare Access can put a sign-in in front of it. A public address is also what a web app such as claude.ai needs to connect to Kept’s MCP server.

cloudflared, like the other tunnels here, reaches Kept from the same machine; trust it as in reverse proxies.

Your own reverse proxy
Section titled “Your own reverse proxy”

Any proxy that terminates TLS and forwards to port 8080 works. Read reverse proxies for the three settings that matter.

A certificate only your devices trust
Section titled “A certificate only your devices trust”

On a LAN with no domain, mkcert can make a certificate for the machine’s address, served through any TLS proxy. Every phone must then trust mkcert’s root certificate; on an iPhone that means installing it as a profile and turning on full trust in Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings. Tailscale is usually less work.

## Backups | Kept
URL: https://keptinventory.info/admin/backups/
Description: Nightly encrypted restic snapshots of the database, the files and a readable copy, to another disk, an S3 bucket or an SFTP server.

Skip to content
Menu
On this page
Overview
Backups

Every night Kept takes one restic snapshot: encrypted with a password you choose, deduplicated (a night with nothing new adds almost nothing), and sent to a place that isn’t the server’s own disk.

What a snapshot holds
Section titled “What a snapshot holds”
The database, dumped from one consistent moment, with a manifest of every table’s row count and a digest of its data, so a restore can prove it brought back exactly what was there.
The files (photos, receipts, documents), when they are stored on the server’s disk. With S3 file storage they aren’t: see below.
A readable copy of every location: web pages, spreadsheets, thumbnails and receipts that open in a browser with nothing but restic. See read your inventory with restic alone.

The keys are not in the backup. Keep the recovery kit somewhere else.

Where it can go
Section titled “Where it can go”
Target	Set with	The restic repository
A directory: another disk, or a NAS share mounted on the server	KEPT_BACKUP_DIR (absolute, outside KEPT_DATA_DIR)	<directory>/restic
An S3-compatible bucket: AWS, or another provider’s S3 endpoint	KEPT_BACKUP_S3_BUCKET and the other KEPT_BACKUP_S3_*	restic/ under KEPT_BACKUP_S3_PREFIX
An SFTP server	KEPT_BACKUP_SFTP (restic’s sftp: syntax), KEPT_BACKUP_SFTP_KEY_FILE, KEPT_BACKUP_SFTP_KNOWN_HOSTS	the location you give

Set one target. Prefer another machine or another site: a directory on the same disk as Kept’s data is refused, and the status page warns when the target shares a disk with it. Backblaze B2’s and Cloudflare R2’s S3 endpoints are expected to work but haven’t been tested. SFTP pins the server’s host key from the known-hosts file and connects only if it matches.

Turning it on
Section titled “Turning it on”

Instance admins set the target and the password in Admin → Backups, over HTTPS, after acknowledging the recovery kit. “Test” checks Kept can open (or create) the repository; “Run now” runs one at once. An environment variable beats the screen and shows there as locked, so an operator can fix the target in the deployment.

The password is at least 12 characters (KEPT_BACKUP_PASSWORD, or set on the screen). No password, no backup: Kept never writes an unencrypted backup. Lose the password and the backup is unreadable, which is why it is in the recovery kit.

The backup runs in the worker as the database owner, so the worker needs KEPT_OWNER_DATABASE_URL as well. With Compose, compose.yaml already passes every KEPT_BACKUP_* variable from .env to Kept and to migrate (which takes a snapshot before an upgrade); a compose.override.yaml next to it adds the owner login and, for a directory target, the mount on both:

services:
  kept:
    environment:
      KEPT_OWNER_DATABASE_URL: postgres://kept_owner:${KEPT_DB_OWNER_PASSWORD:-}@db:5432/kept
      KEPT_DB_OWNER_PASSWORD_FILE: /owner/kept_owner
    volumes:
      - kept-owner:/owner:ro
      - /mnt/backup/kept:/backups
  migrate:
    volumes:
      - /mnt/backup/kept:/backups

The owner’s password comes from the kept-owner volume, where the bootstrap keeps it (an install from before 1.13.0 with KEPT_DB_OWNER_PASSWORD in .env uses that instead, and the file line does nothing).

Then either set the target and the password on the screen, or lock them in .env (KEPT_BACKUP_DIR=/backups, KEPT_BACKUP_PASSWORD=…).

The directory must belong to Kept’s user:

Terminal window
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/backup/kept
sudo chown 10001:10001 /mnt/backup/kept
sudo chmod 700 /mnt/backup/kept
When and how long
Section titled “When and how long”
When: every night at the time set in Admin → Backups, HH:MM in UTC (default 02:30). A new time applies from the next night, with no restart; KEPT_BACKUP_TIME fixes it instead.
Run now runs one at once; pressing it again while that one waits or runs is refused (“A backup is already running”) rather than queued twice. A backup cut off by a restart or by running out of memory doesn’t block it; the next run marks that one interrupted.
On a small machine (under 4 GB, or a container limit under 4 GB) restic runs on at most two cores with a soft memory limit; GOMAXPROCS and GOMEMLIMIT in Kept’s environment (with Compose, a compose.override.yaml) override both.
How long they’re kept: the newest snapshot of each of the last 7 days, 4 weeks and 6 months (KEPT_BACKUP_KEEP_DAILY, _WEEKLY, _MONTHLY). The alpha’s KEPT_BACKUP_KEEP is read as the daily count for one release. Snapshots taken before an upgrade keep their last 3.
A suspiciously small backup (a dump under half the last good one’s size, or far fewer things, places or files) is still taken, but nothing old is removed that night and admins are alerted, so a bad night can never push the good snapshots out.
Watching it
Section titled “Watching it”

Admin → Status shows the last backup and its age, the number of snapshots, the repository’s size, the last restore drill, and the disks. Admins are alerted by mail and push when:

Alert	When
Backup failed	a run fails
Backup stale	no good backup for 36 hours with a target set
Suspicious size	a run was much smaller than the last good one
Disk space low	the data disk or a directory target is 85 % full
Bucket versioning off	files are in S3 and the bucket keeps no old versions
Restore drill due	no restore drill for 30 days

/metrics (with KEPT_METRICS_TOKEN) adds the last good backup’s time and the disks’ use. See monitoring.

When files live in S3
Section titled “When files live in S3”

restic backs up files on disk, not objects in a bucket. With KEPT_STORAGE=s3, the snapshot holds the database, the manifest and the readable copy, and the bucket keeps the files safe itself: turn on bucket versioning (and, if your provider has it, replication to another region). Kept checks versioning on every run and alerts while it is off. The weekly check and the restore drill compare every file’s hash in the manifest with the bucket.

The alpha’s backups
Section titled “The alpha’s backups”

Backups made before restic, by the alpha (runs/ and blobs/ beside the new restic/ directory), are never written again, and stay restorable with kept admin restore --legacy <id> for one release. Delete them once a restic snapshot has passed a restore drill.

## Connect an AI client (MCP) | Kept
URL: https://keptinventory.info/users/mcp-clients/
Description: Connect Claude Desktop or another AI agent to Kept's MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, with a personal token or OAuth.

Skip to content
Menu
On this page
Overview
Connect an AI client (MCP)

Kept runs an MCP server at your Kept’s address followed by /mcp, for example https://kept.example.org/mcp. An AI app that speaks MCP can then answer “where is the drill?” from your inventory and, if you allow it, add, move and change things.

This page is about apps outside Kept. Kept’s own assistant uses the same tools and is covered in AI providers. How the server works inside is in MCP server.

There are two ways to connect an app:

A personal token: any MCP client that lets you set a server address and an Authorization header.
A connector (OAuth): the app sends you to Kept to sign in and choose what it may do. This needs Kept at an https address the app can reach.

Not yet checked against the apps

Kept’s tests connect an MCP client both ways. Checks against claude.ai, ChatGPT and Claude Desktop themselves are still pending, so it isn’t yet confirmed which of them connect as connectors.

Before you start
Section titled “Before you start”
Turn on “Connect ChatGPT or Claude” in each location the app should reach. It is under Location settings → What to track, and is on in the Complete preset only. The owner and admins change it. In a location where it’s off, a token or connector reaches nothing.
The app makes tokens only over https. Settings → Connections refuses to make a token when KEPT_PUBLIC_URL is plain http. There is no setting to turn this off. See HTTPS. On a home network over http, the person who runs the server can make one there instead: kept admin token create.
Make a personal token
Section titled “Make a personal token”

Open Settings → Connections and choose New token.

Field	What to put
Name	Where you’ll use it: “Claude Desktop, my laptop”.
Locations	One is ticked for you. Add another only if the app needs both.
What it can do	Read only: find things and read what’s recorded. Read and change: also add, move or change them. Neither can delete or see secret fields.
Expires	A date, or empty to keep it until you revoke it. It ends at the end of that day.

Then Make token. A token never does more than you can: where you’re a viewer, it can only read. A token that can change things in several locations whose members differ gets a warning, Different people use these locations, because an app could then move things from one to another. Make it for all of them goes ahead; one token per location is the safer choice.

The token, kpt_ followed by two parts, appears once, with Copy. Kept keeps only a fingerprint of it, so a lost token can’t be shown again: revoke it and make another.

In a location that requires two-factor, a token works only if you made it while signed in with your second factor.

Connect a client with the token
Section titled “Connect a client with the token”

Under the new token, Connect an app shows two values, each with a copy button:

Server address   https://kept.example.org/mcp
Authorization    Bearer kpt_…

In the app, add an MCP server (it may be called a connector or an integration) with that address, and send the token in that header. Kept doesn’t supply a settings file for any particular app; where the address and header go is in the app’s own documentation.

The endpoint answers POST only, keeps no session between requests, and refuses a request whose Host isn’t Kept’s address (or one it used before) or that comes from another website’s page.

Connect as a connector (OAuth)
Section titled “Connect as a connector (OAuth)”

Apps that support it can connect without a token you copy. This is on by itself when KEPT_PUBLIC_URL is https. Admin → Status → Connections from other apps shows the MCP endpoint and either Available or Needs an https public URL.

In the app, add https://kept.example.org/mcp as a connector.
The app finds Kept’s sign-in from the address and sends you to Kept. Sign in.
Kept shows App wants to use your Kept. The name is the one the app gives itself; Kept can’t confirm who made it. Choose What it can do and Where (pick only the locations it needs), then Allow or Deny. The page also says the app stays signed in after you sign out of this browser, and that anything that signs out all your other devices makes it sign in again.
The app appears under Connected apps in Settings → Connections.

The app stays connected until you press Revoke on it and confirm (Kept asks Disconnect App?), or until it goes 30 days without being used; then it has to sign in again. Each access token it gets lasts an hour and the app renews it without asking you again; Kept checks your grant on every call, so Revoke in Settings → Connections works at once.

The app has to sign in again after anything that signs out your other devices: Sign out of all other devices, a new password or a password reset, a change to two-factor, backup codes or passkeys, unlinking an outside sign-in, a new email address, or an admin signing you out everywhere or disabling your account. Signing out one chosen device leaves the app signed in.

One exception: asking to delete your account signs out your other devices but keeps the app’s sign-in. The app stops working while the account waits, and if you keep the account, it works again without signing in.

Things that stop a connector:

The app can’t reach Kept. A web app such as claude.ai connects from its own servers, so Kept must be reachable from the internet, not only on your home network or tailnet.
Kept can’t reach the app. An app identifies itself with an https address for a document describing it, and Kept fetches that document. Private and local addresses are refused.
The app registers itself. Kept accepts apps that describe themselves with such a document (Client ID Metadata Documents) and has dynamic client registration turned off. An app that can only register dynamically can’t connect as a connector; use a personal token if it accepts one.
What an app can and can’t do
Section titled “What an app can and can’t do”
It sees only the locations you picked, and in each only the tools for the parts of Kept that location has on. Where your role hides values, they’re hidden from the app too.
Changes apply at once and are listed under Recent changes by connections on the Connections page, with Undo for 7 days. Undo refuses when the field has changed since.
There is nothing destructive to call. No tool deletes, trashes, merges, transfers ownership, reveals a secret field, uploads a file or runs a query of its own.
Files go through you. attach_link gives the app a link that opens Kept’s capture sheet; you add the photo or receipt there, signed in.
Limits per token: 120 reads and 30 changes a minute. Answers are short and paged, 20 items unless the app asks for more, up to 200.
Text people wrote is marked as untrusted. Names and notes reach the app under an untrusted key, and Kept tells it never to follow instructions found in them.
The tools
Section titled “The tools”

An app sees only the tools it may call in each location; capabilities lists them. Hiding Personal doesn’t change what an app was given. Read tools work with either kind of access; change tools need Read and change and a role of member or higher. The part of Kept a tool needs is the name under What to track.

Tool	Kind	Needs	What it answers
capabilities	read		What can I do in each location: its parts and the tools I may call there.
list_locations	read		Which locations can I see, with my role and their time zone.
search_things	read		Which things match these words: names, aliases, types, brands and notes, with filters.
where_is	read		Where is a thing: the best matches with their full place path.
get_thing	read		What do we know about this thing (by id or short ID), who has it, and a kit’s parts.
list_contents	read		What is in this place or container, 1 to 3 levels deep.
thing_history	read		What happened to this thing, newest first: who did what and when.
find_documents	read		Where is the receipt, manual or warranty for something.
upcoming	read	Reminders	What is due, overdue or expiring soon: schedules, warranties, loans and low stock.
add_thing	change		Add one or more things, with a new place if it doesn’t exist yet, and every field the app’s create sheet sets (see below).
update_thing	change		Change any of a thing’s fields the app’s edit form changes (see below); null clears one.
move_thing	change		Move a thing, or some of a quantity, to another place or container.
mark_seen	change		I just saw this thing where Kept says it is.
create_place	change		Add a place under another place, or at the top of the location. With template, add furniture and a place for each of its compartments in one step, as Furniture with compartments does; one Undo takes it all back. A room takes its real size, width_cm and length_cm (50 cm to 100 m), and goes on the map with it.
update_place	change		Change a place as its page does: rename it, change its kind, move it into another place or to the top, set its fields, and the order of the places in it (A to Z or Custom order, then Move up or Move down). turn (right or left, where its top went) turns furniture with compartments onto its side or back, with renumber true or false. Undo for 7 days, except a move up or down: the opposite move undoes it.
turn_into_boxes	change		Turn up to 50 places into boxes, as Turn places into boxes does. Each keeps its ID, label and what’s in it; one with places inside stays a place, and so does one at the top of the location (turn that one in Kept). One Undo turns them all back.
attach_link	change		A link that opens Kept’s capture sheet to add a photo, receipt or document.
log_reading	change		Record a meter reading: odometer, hours, electricity.
lend_thing	change	Lending	Lend a thing to someone, with an optional due date. A box or a kit goes with everything in it, each on its own line.
return_thing	change	Lending	A lent or borrowed thing came back, all of it or a quantity. A box or kit brings back what is still out with it.
borrow_thing	change	Lending	Record a thing borrowed from someone, with an optional due date.
complete_schedule	change	Reminders	A scheduled task was done, on a date or at a meter value.
snooze_schedule	change	Reminders	Put off a scheduled task until a date or a meter value.
add_warranty	change	Receipts and warranties	Record a warranty: its kind, and when it ends or how many months.
open_claim	change	Receipts and warranties	Open a warranty claim for a thing.
update_claim	change	Receipts and warranties	Change a claim’s status or reference.
log_service	change		Record a service: date, who did it, total, lines (each may use stock from a consumable), the schedules it completes, and notes.
log_fuel	change	Fuel	Record a fill-up: amount, unit, cost, whether full, and the odometer.
adjust_stock	change	Things you run out of	Add to or take from a consumable’s stock.
list_tags	read		Which tags there are, with how many things have each.
tag_things	change		Add tags to things, or take them off; a new name makes the tag.
list_moves	read	Moving house	Which moves there are, with how many boxes are packed, in transit and unpacked.
get_move	read	Moving house	Where each box of a move is, and which numbers are still missing.
start_move	change	Moving house	Start a move, to another location or between rooms of this one.
add_box	change	Moving house	Add the next numbered box: a new one, or a container you have.
pack_into_box	change	Moving house	Pack things into a box.
set_box_status	change	Moving house	Mark a box packed or in transit, or choose its room.
unpack_box	change	Moving house	Unpack a box into a room; everything in it goes with it.

A thing’s fields. add_thing and update_thing take every field you can set on a thing in the app, each in its own field rather than in the notes: name, how many, type (by name, in English or Arabic, or by id), brand (made if new), model, serial number, barcode, colour, condition, notes, other names, tags (a new name makes the tag, for members and up), whose it is (a person, made if new), the manual’s link, expir
